desc:
Every cell of the grid holds an arrow: 1 points right, 2 points left, 3 points down and 4 points up. A traveller starts in the top-left cell and, in each step, moves to the neighbouring cell in the direction of the arrow in the cell they stand on. The walk is meant to end in the bottom-right cell.

You may change the arrow in any cell to any of the four directions; changing one cell costs 1 (a cell is changed at most once). Arrows are allowed to point out of the grid as long as the traveller never actually follows such an arrow.

Return the minimum number of cells you must change so that the traveller starting in the top-left cell reaches the bottom-right cell.

grid = [[1,1,3],
        [2,4,2],
        [1,1,1]]  -> 1   (redirect the arrow in the middle of the right column)
grid = [[2,2],
        [2,2]]    -> 2
grid = [[4]]       -> 0
hints: Think of cells as nodes of a graph: from each cell you can step to its up to four neighbours. What does a step cost?
A step in the direction of the cell's own arrow is free, any other step costs 1 (you change the arrow). So you want the cheapest path where every edge costs 0 or 1.

Use Dijkstra, or the faster 0-1 BFS: keep a deque, push a neighbour reached by a cost-0 edge at the front and one reached by a cost-1 edge at the back. The distance of the bottom-right cell is the answer.
editorial: Model the grid as a weighted graph: from cell (r, c) there is an edge to each in-grid neighbour, with weight 0 if the arrow in (r, c) points to that neighbour and weight 1 otherwise. A path of total weight W corresponds to a plan that changes exactly W arrows along that path. Conversely, any plan for which the traveller arrives walks along a path that never repeats a cell (a repeat would make the traveller loop forever), so its number of changes is at least the weight of that path. Hence the answer is the shortest path from the top-left to the bottom-right cell.

With only weights 0 and 1, Dijkstra's heap is unnecessary. In 0-1 BFS you use a double-ended queue: when relaxing an edge of weight 0, push the neighbour on the front, otherwise on the back. The deque then always holds nodes in nondecreasing distance order (it contains at most two distinct distance values), exactly like BFS does for unit weights.
Each cell is relaxed a bounded number of times, so the time is O(rows × cols). When processing a popped cell, read its current best distance from the table, because a cell may be pushed twice.
